cover.art_brief: A small market town in the valley (timber, wattle and thatch, a little stone church tower behind; valley greens and slate), market day in sunshine. In the far background, by a big house with a hanging bush sign (no lettering), a black horse is tied. No text, no numbers.

grammar.nodyn_en:
This chapter counts. The numbers from one to ten are un, dau, tri, pedwar, pump, chwech, saith, wyth, naw, deg, as Modlen counts her eggs, and ugain is twenty: Ugain ceiniog ('Twenty pennies'). Eleven is un ar ddeg, already met in the age phrase of Pennod 8: bachgen un ar ddeg oed ('an eleven-year-old boy').

In the direct number + noun pattern shown here, Welsh uses the singular noun, not the plural: deg wy ('ten eggs', not wyau), naw afal ('nine apples'), saith ceiniog ('seven pennies'), deg bachgen ('ten boys'). When referring to several eggs, pennies or apples without a numeral, use their plural forms: yr wyau ('the eggs'), y ceiniogau ('the pennies'), yr afalau ('the apples'). A number can also stand alone when the noun is clear: Mae Elen yn rhoi dwy geiniog i Arth, a dwy i Mali ('Elen gives two pennies to Arth, and two to Mali').

Every Welsh noun is either masculine or feminine; the vocabulary marks them (g.) and (b.). Two, three and four have a separate feminine form, used with feminine nouns: dau afal ('two apples') but dwy geiniog ('two pennies'), tri chaws ('three cheeses') but tair ceiniog ('three pennies'), pedwar mochyn ('four pigs') but pedair dafad ('four sheep'). In this chapter ceiniog ('penny'), dafad ('sheep') and buwch ('cow') are feminine; afal ('apple'), wy ('egg'), caws ('cheese') and mochyn ('pig') are masculine. The other numbers have one form for both genders, though un treats them differently, as below.

Some numbers change the first sound of the next word. Un ('one') gives a feminine singular noun the soft mutation, the softening of a word's first sound met after yn and y: un geiniog ('one penny', from ceiniog). A masculine noun stays as it is: un bachgen ('one boy'). As after yn, a feminine noun beginning with ll- or rh- does not soften after un. Dau and dwy soften the noun after them: dau gaws ('two cheeses', from caws), dwy geiniog ('two pennies'). Tair and pedair do not: tair ceiniog, pedair ceiniog.

Tri and chwe cause the aspirate mutation, which changes only c, p and t (to ch, ph and th): tri chaws ('three cheeses', from caws), chwe cheiniog ('six pennies', from ceiniog). The story shows only c → ch. A word beginning with any other sound stays as it is: tri afal ('three apples').

When counting, five and six are pump and chwech. Before a noun they shorten to pum and chwe: pum ceiniog ('five pennies'), chwe cheiniog ('six pennies'). Mali adds up the wool like this: Tair ceiniog a dwy geiniog: pum ceiniog, dim saith! ('Three pennies and two pennies: five pennies, not seven!').

A number can itself be softened by the word before it, like any other word. After dyma: Dyma dair ceiniog ('Here are three pennies', from tair). As the thing asked for after Gaf i: Gaf i ddau afal? ('May I have two apples?', from dau).

Faint yw …? asks a price: Faint yw'r caws? ('How much is the cheese?') Tair ceiniog ('Three pennies'). Faint yw'r mochyn bach? ('How much is the little pig?') Ugain ceiniog ('Twenty pennies'). As the examples show, the answer can be just the amount.

Gaf i …? ('May I have …?') asks for something. It is a question form of cael ('to get, to have'), with its first sound softened, like Gest ti …? in Pennod 13. The answers are Cei ('Yes, you may') and Na chei ('No, you may not'), where na changes the c of cei to ch: Gaf i afal? Cei ('May I have an apple? Yes'); Modlen, gaf i fochyn bach? Na chei! ('Modlen, may I have a little pig? No!'). The thing asked for is the object, so it softens as objects did in Pennod 13: fochyn from mochyn, ddau from dau.
